name: Inpainting and Canvas Expansion
title: Inpainting and Canvas Expansion
answer: Inpainting is the process of filling a masked or missing region of an image with generated content that matches its surroundings. Canvas expansion, often called outpainting, extends an image beyond its original borders by generating new pixels that continue the existing composition. Both sit inside generative illustration, where artists use them to repair, recompose, or enlarge a picture without repainting it by hand. The work ranges from small touch ups to building a wider scene from a narrow crop.

sections.body: Inpainting is the process of filling a masked or missing region of an image with generated content that matches its surroundings. Canvas expansion, often called outpainting, extends an image beyond its original borders by generating new pixels that continue the existing composition. Both sit inside generative illustration, where artists use them to repair, recompose, or enlarge a picture without repainting it by hand. The work ranges from small touch ups to building a wider scene from a narrow crop.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These operations run on the same hardware as other image generation: GPUs, either local or cloud, with enough video memory to hold the model and the image at the working resolution. Latent diffusion models are common, because they operate in a compressed space that makes large canvases more tractable. Tiling and patch based methods let a system expand an image in steps, so memory use stays bounded. The site tracks 1000 live image generation models, and inpainting or outpainting is a standard mode in that class of system.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The usual workflow starts with a mask that marks the area to be filled or the new region to be added. A model then generates content conditioned on the unmasked pixels, often with a text prompt or reference image to guide style and subject. For canvas expansion, the system may generate in overlapping tiles and blend the seams, or use a model trained to continue edges and textures. Artists iterate by adjusting the mask, the prompt, and the blend, then retouch the result in a standard image editor. Some pipelines use a separate refinement pass to improve coherence at the boundary.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and provenance are central because inpainting can alter an existing work and canvas expansion can create new content that may resemble training data. The site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, a reminder that generated or extended imagery can become part of a dispute over ownership or infringement. Provenance tools, such as signed metadata or watermarks, are sometimes used to record that a region was generated. Artists and studios often keep records of source images, masks, prompts, and model versions to show how a final image was made.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more controllable and higher resolution expansion, with models that understand perspective, lighting, and object continuity across a larger canvas. Interactive tools are becoming faster, so artists can expand a canvas in real time and see the result before committing. There is also work on consistency across multiple expansions, so a scene can grow in several directions without drifting in style. As these methods improve, the line between editing an existing image and generating a new one continues to blur.
